extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate, graduate, and early-career mathematicians (students, postdocs) considering or pursuing academic careers in mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of career and research-life advice for people at different stages (undergraduate, graduate, postdoc) aiming for academic research careers in mathematics, covering study habits, research strategy, presentation, and time management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work hard
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to work hard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises sustained effort as a core requirement for progress in graduate and research careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work professionally
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt professional habits and standards in research and collaboration (e.g., reliability, meeting deadlines, clear communication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoy your work
rubrics_metrics.description: But it is also important to enjoy your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic enjoyment helps sustain long-term research activity; balance hard work with engagement in topics you find rewarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think ahead to understand the way forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Think ahead to understand the way forward; ask yourself dumb questions to understand the way before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan research direction and next steps; use simple/basic questions to clarify understanding before attempting advanced moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks and conferences broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend talks and conferences, even those not directly related to your own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose yourself to broader ideas, techniques, and potential collaborators beyond your immediate subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to your advisor but take initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to your advisor, but also take the initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your advisor's guidance while proactively shaping your research agenda and seeking opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't prematurely obsess on a single 'big problem' or 'big theory'
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't prematurely obsess on a single “big problem” or “big theory”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid locking into one grand aim too early; explore, build tools, and gain perspective before committing to a long risky project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down what you've done and make your work available
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down what you’ve done, and make your work available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep records, write drafts, circulate preprints; making progress and partial results visible helps feedback and career development. (See linked advice on how to write and submit papers.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and relearn your field; continue learning outside your field
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn and relearn your field, but don't be afraid to learn things outside your field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously refresh core knowledge while acquiring complementary skills and techniques from other areas to broaden applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn limitations of your tools and learn the power of others' tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the limitations of your tools, but also learn the power of other mathematician’s tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know where your current methods fail and when to adopt different approaches; survey other techniques to extend your range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim just beyond your current range
rubrics_metrics.description: In particular, you should continually aim just beyond your current range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose projects that stretch your abilities but remain achievable; incremental stretching fosters growth without excessive risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible and patient in research
rubrics_metrics.description: In your research, be both flexible and patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to change direction when needed and accept that progress often takes time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel and present research when opportunities arise; tailor talks to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: You should definitely travel and present your research if given the opportunity. But be considerate of your audience; talks are not the same as papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take chances to present work for visibility and feedback; adapt content and style for talks (more exposition and intuition) versus written papers (precision, full proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of your own work; use the wastebasket
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sceptical of your own work, and don’t be afraid to use the wastebasket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate and discard or shelve ideas that don't pan out; pruning ideas is a normal part of research productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Batch low-intensity tasks together
rubrics_metrics.description: Batch low-intensity tasks together to take advantage of economies of scale and to reduce distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group administrative or small tasks into focused blocks to reduce context switching and preserve deep-work time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value partial progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Value partial progress, as a crucial stepping stone to a complete solution of a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and record intermediate results or lemmas; incremental progress is meaningful and builds toward major results.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is more to mathematics than grades, exams, rigour, and proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that there is more to maths than grades and exams and methods; there is also more to maths than rigour and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden training beyond formal exercises: cultivate intuition, problem selection, exposition, and creativity, not just formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't base career decisions on glamour or fame; study at different places
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t base career decisions on glamour or fame. But you should study at different places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make pragmatic choices about programs and advisors rather than chasing reputation alone; experience at multiple institutions can broaden perspective and opportunities.
